FAST

SEOUL, Nov 3 : South Korea's headline inflation slowed in October, government data showed on Tuesday, providing a slight reprieve for central bankers but remaining firmly above target. Consumer prices rose 2.8 per cent year-on-year in October, down from a 2.9 per cent gain in September and nearly matching a 2.85 per cent increase forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. The consumer price index rose 0.2 per cent on a monthly basis after gaining 0.3 per cent in the previous month, the data showed. While the slower growth offers the Bank of Korea a brief respite, inflation remains well above its 2.0 per cent target. Amid elevated global energy prices and rising household borrowing, the BOK is widely expected to hike rates in the coming months, maintaining its tight monetary posture to calm persistent inflationary pressures in Asia’s fourth-largest economy. A separate poll showed consensus forecasts put the peak policy interest rate at 3.50 per cent, which prices in one more hike this November and another in the first quarter of 2027.

Source: Reuters

ORLANDO, Florida, Nov 2 : Oil prices tumbled on Monday on hopes that US-Iran peace talks could soon take place, which pushed bond yields around the world lower. Stock markets in Asia and Europe mostly benefited as a result, but the momentum evaporated in US hours, as investors turned their attention to Tuesday's midterm elections. In my column today, I look at the impact an AI-driven stock market rout could have on economic growth. It would vary from country to country, of course, but negative wealth effects and lower AI capex could stir recession fears across the developed world. Today's Key Reads • Investors gaming out Congress control for spending, AI outlook

• Sectors bracing for a pivot as US midterm elections loom • US Treasury auction changes loom in 2027; dealers eye long-end cuts • New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe • Manufacturing solid but strain of energy costs, supply disruptions starts to show • Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: South Korea +2 per cent, Japan -0.3 per cent. Europe +0.4 per cent, UK +0.3 per cent. Brazil -0.8 per cent, down every trading day since October 26 election. Nasdaq -1 per cent, S&P 500 -0.5 per cent, Dow +0.4 per cent.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Consumer cyclicals +2 per cent, tech -2.7 per cent, energy -4 per cent. Apple trade choppy after results, Palantir +3 per cent. Alphabet slips again. Marvell -13 per cent, Lumentum -19 per cent after deal.FX: Dollar slips. Norwegian crown biggest G10 FX decliner, slumps more than 1 per cent. Swiss franc biggest G10 climber, +1 per cent. Chilean peso up nearly 2 per cent.BONDS: UK gilt yields -10 bps. US yields -4 bps at long end, curve flattens for the first day in four.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil -8 per cent, Brent's biggest fall since April. WTI's since July. Gold +2 per cent, still below $4,000. Today's Talking Points: Oil, election, & bluff? Crude oil prices had their biggest one-day fall in months on Monday, as hope spread that Iran may be more open to negotiations with the US to end the war. This comes on the eve of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump's Republican Party is expected to fare badly, in large part because of the unpopularity of the war and the high energy prices it has caused. Could this wave of peace talk optimism finally be the one that is backed up with actual progress? Trump has previously signaled new attacks on Iran could follow the midterms, and he may face additional pressure from Israel to stay on the offensive. But on Monday he appeared to soften his stance, and said a deal "could happen". Things might become a little clearer after Tuesday's elections. At least, that's the hope. Cyber pass The AI trade has faltered recently mainly due to growing worries that companies are borrowing too much to fund a capex binge that might simply be too big. AI's potential existential threats to humanity have sparked intense debate, but these are risks that are almost impossible to price into asset values. In the same vein, cybersecurity risks are also difficult to quantify, but if AI increases the potential for cyberattacks, investors will have to prepare accordingly. And soon. Hackers stole more than $6 billion last week from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, prompting the exchange's customers to withdraw nearly $5 billion. The theft, potentially the largest-ever financial heist, underlines the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks. But it's not just crypto that's vulnerable. Hackers attacked fridges and freezers in supermarkets across Europe on Monday, forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month. Is AI a help or hindrance in the battle for cybersecurity? Central bank fest, part II After the Fed, ECB and BOJ last week, investors have another heavy dose of central bank policy decisions and guidance to absorb this week. The Reserve Bank of Australia kicks it off on Tuesday with an expected rate hike to 4.85 per cent, which would be its fifth this year. Decisions from Sweden, Poland, Brazil, Norway, the UK and Mexico follow. If there is a unifying theme, it is inflation, although price pressures aren't uniform. And nor is policymakers' reaction function — the RBA and Norges Bank have been hiking rates this year, while the BoE hasn't started yet. In Brazil, policymakers suddenly have to face a very different financial market environment following last month's presidential election. Watch out for some punchy FX moves this week, especially in the Brazilian real. FAST

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 2 : Apple on Monday forecast lower gross margins for the crucial holiday quarter, citing rising memory-chip costs, and projected services revenue growth that fell well short of Wall Street expectations. Shares of the iPhone maker, which were little changed in after-hours trading after it reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that beat expectations, fell 4 per cent during a conference call after executives outlined the weaker outlook. The quarter was boosted by early demand for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and higher prices. Apple said it expects gross margin of 45 per cent to 46 per cent in the quarter ending in December, down from 47.9 per cent in the fourth quarter. It forecast services revenue growth of 8 per cent to 9 per cent, below analysts' expectations of 10.7 per cent. The results and forecast come as Apple experiments with a string of firsts under new CEO John Ternus, who took over in September. After nearly two decades of launching most of its new iPhones each autumn, Apple this year is spacing those out, with iPhone Pro and Duo models shipping this year and other iPhone models expected next year.

Apple also released a bevy of new non-iPhone products in the current holiday shopping quarter, including its first touchscreen laptops and its first smart-home hub. The steady drumbeat of releases, analysts said, is meant to smooth out Apple's yearly revenue cycle, which for decades showed a huge boom in holiday-quarter sales of new iPhones that petered out by late summer as consumers came to anticipate new models. Apple in recent weeks has grappled with customer reports of cracked screens on the iPhone Duo, the company's first foldable phone, which sold out within hours online and spurred lines at Apple's stores last month. Apple said fiscal fourth-quarter sales were $114.48 billion, above analyst estimates of $113.39 billion, according to LSEG data. Profit  for the fourth quarter was $2.10 per share, above analyst estimates of $1.99 per share even when excluding 5 cents per share from tariff refunds. IPHONE DUO SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS In an interview with Reuters, Ternus said that "a very small percentage" of iPhone Duo units had been returned for display issues and that Apple is replacing them. He said the company is overall unable to meet demand for the devices, with no timeline for when Apple will catch up. "Duo is constrained as of today," Ternus said. "The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance."  Apple said that fourth-quarter iPhone sales, which included iPhone 18 Pro models but not Duo sales, were $57.58 billion, above analyst estimates of $56.54 billion, according to LSEG data. The strategy change comes as Apple faces headwinds from an AI-driven memory-chip price spike that previous CEO Tim Cook likened to a 100-year flood that could dampen the margin boost that Apple derives from selling storage upgrades. “The big question for Apple moving forward will be how well they can weather the significant component price  increases that have slowed their PC and smartphone competitors," said Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. "The new iPhone Duo looks to be a big hit, but the company has to solve the screen glitches and ramp up its manufacturing output before it can make a significant impact on the bottom line.” PRICE RISES OFFSET CHIP COSTS As it launched its new iPhone 18 Pro models, Apple also increased the price of iPhone 17 models by $100 and increased some MacBook prices, helping soften the blow of memory-chip prices that continued to rise. "We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," Ternus told Reuters. "These price increases provided some offset." Apple said that gross margins were 47.9 per cent, above analyst estimates of 47.5 per cent, according to LSEG data. Another key question for Apple's margins is the costs of its new AI-infused Siri, which Ternus said is now fielding 2.5 billion requests per day. "Now we have the Siri that we always wanted, which we really built from the ground up," Ternus said. Apple said that sales of its Mac computers, which have gained popularity among tech enthusiasts as a platform for hosting AI agents, were $10.79 billion, above estimates of $9.61 billion. Services revenue was $31.57 billion, in line with analyst estimates of $31.58 billion, according to LSEG data. Sales of iPads and wearables were $6.23 billion and $8.30 billion, respectively, both below estimates of $6.70 billion and $9.06 billion, respectively.

Source: Reuters

Nov 2 : Tinder's daily active users in the US returned to annual growth in October, parent Match Group's chief financial officer told Reuters on Monday, a key milestone in the dating app's turnaround efforts. Improvements in DAU were largely driven by better algorithms, helped by the use of AI to analyze unstructured data and identify more compatible users, finance chief Steve Bailey said, without disclosing the monthly numbers. Tinder's global DAU had returned to year-over-year growth in September for the first time in three and a half years. Dating apps have turned to AI as younger Gen Z users' growing disillusionment with endless swiping fuels weaker user engagement.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to be between $2.649 billion and $2.653 billion, it said on Monday, above LSEG-compiled analysts' average estimate of $2.46 billion. However, shares fell nearly 3 per cent in extended trading. "On the negative side, some investors may be disappointed with the US commercial bookings," William Blair analysts said.

Palantir said it signed multiple eight-figure deals in the quarter that were "shorter in duration than usual" as customers rapidly adopted initial sovereign AI capabilities, which allow enterprises to retain control over their data and how AI is deployed and used. In the third quarter, revenue from commercial clients surpassed government revenue in the US for the first time, driven by the rapid adoption of AI software to improve operations and safeguard sensitive data. Palantir, which develops the Maven Smart System used by NATO's military headquarters and several European armed forces, built its business around government and defense contracts. Total quarterly revenue jumped about 96 per cent to $2.31 billion, the second straight quarter of 90 per cent growth. Analysts had estimated revenue of $2.18 billion. US commercial revenue was $984 million, while US government revenue came in at $953 million during the period. The company reported a total of 1,090 customers in the trailing 12-month period ending September 30, with 904 classified as commercial. Palantir also raised its annual revenue expectations to between $8.530 billion and $8.534 billion, up from its prior estimates of between $8.150 billion and $8.158 billion.

Nov 2 : Scientists have discovered what they consider the strongest evidence yet of blood cells in a dinosaur fossil inside bone from the right leg of a medium-sized meat-eater that prowled Brazil some 115 million years ago during the Cretaceous Period. The researchers identified numerous microscopic structures in bone from the species Aratasaurus museunacionali that appear to be fossilized red blood cells. They also detected chemical evidence related to a key component of these cells — an iron-containing biomolecule called heme that is associated with hemoglobin, the protein that gives blood its red color. The evidence for blood cells and heme was found in vascular canals inside bones of an Aratasaurus individual, thought to be a juvenile or young adult about 4 years old when it died. The bipedal dinosaur would have measured about 10 feet (3.1 meters) long. "We have not found a vial of dinosaur blood. What we are seeing is a mineral and molecular echo of ancient biology, and that is scientifically much more interesting," said Kliti Grice, an organic and isotope geochemist at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and lead author of the study published on Monday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

"For me, the most surprising thing is that we can see the structures together with chemical evidence of their biological origin after such enormous geological time," Grice said. Red blood cells, continuously manufactured inside bone marrow, transport oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and then help bring carbon dioxide back from the tissues to the lungs to be exhaled. Unlike hard bones and teeth, soft tissues like muscles and feathers are only rarely preserved in fossils. Cells present in bodily liquids like blood are even less commonly spotted in fossils. "Bones and teeth tell us an enormous amount about anatomy, growth and evolution. Molecular and cellular evidence potentially adds another level of biological information," Grice said. The research does not document dinosaur DNA, Grice said, cautioning against interpreting the discovery as evidence that intact dinosaur genetic material is present. "DNA and other large, information-rich biomolecules have very different preservation characteristics from small molecules and chemically transformed molecular remnants. The survival of cell-like morphology and heme-related chemical signals does not mean that the DNA that was originally contained within cells has survived," Grice said. 'TESTING THE LIMITS' The researchers also detected collagen-related amino acids in the Aratasaurus bone, though Grice noted that this is not equivalent to recovering an intact ancient protein or genetic information. Collagen is an abundant structural protein, sort of the scaffolding that holds the body's tissues together. "What the work does encourage us to do is keep testing the limits of molecular preservation rather than assuming that all biological information must disappear after a particular length of time," Grice said. The oldest-known DNA reported by scientists came from animals, plants and microbes dating to about 2 million years ago from sediment in Greenland. The Aratasaurus fossil was unearthed in a gypsum mine in Ceará state in northeastern Brazil, according to paleontologist and study co-author Alexander Kellner of the National Museum of Brazil. It includes parts of the right femur, tibia and foot. "What we believe is distinctive about the present study is the strength of the combined evidence: numerous red-blood-cell-like structures in situ within the dinosaur bone, their mineralization, their location in the vascular system, and associated in situ chemical evidence related to heme. To the best of our knowledge, that combination has not previously been demonstrated in a dinosaur fossil in this way," Grice said.

Source: Reuters

Nov 2 : Meta is eyeing at least $20 billion from a potential cross-border bond offering, Bloomberg News reported on Monday, with the tech giant tapping debt markets again to raise funds for its AI infrastructure build-out. Like many of its tech rivals, Meta has been raising funds through debt and equity to fund the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, though the heavy spending is now attracting heightened investor scrutiny. No final decision has been made and the potential debt offering's size may grow depending on investor demand, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The Facebook parent has asked Citigroup and Morgan Stanley to hold investor calls on Monday and Tuesday, the report added.

Meta, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Meta's potential dollar bond sale will span maturities of 5 to 30 years, while the euro offering will range from around 4 years to just over 38 years, Bloomberg News reported. The debt offering report comes about a week after the company announced plans for its largest-ever equity offerings of around $97.5 billion. The offerings include stock sales of about $37.5 billion it priced last week, and plans to later raise up to $60 billion through an at-the-market share-sale program. Meta had also raised $30 billion in a bond offering last year, and in April sold investment-grade bonds worth $25 billion. The heavy spending on AI infrastructure has weighed on Meta's cash flow, with the company reporting a cash burn of $2.12 billion in the third quarter. S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable", citing significant uncertainty around the company's capital spending and free operating cash flow. Meanwhile, rival Alphabet is selling €6 billion ($6.72 billion) of bonds on Monday, according to a memo from one of the deal's managers. ($1 = 0.8924 euros)

Nov 2 : Snapchat parent Snap Inc has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and eating disorders, attorneys for the plaintiffs said on Monday. Jury selection began last week for the trial, the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Snap, Meta Platforms, TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use. The plaintiffs had previously settled with Meta, TikTok and YouTube. "Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, trial attorneys for plaintiff K.D.B., said in a statement.

The trial was set to be the first for Snap in the sweeping litigation over social media's impact on teens, after the company settled the other cases that had been scheduled for trial. The company's chief executive, Evan Spiegel, had been expected to testify. The case had been selected from thousands of pending lawsuits as a bellwether intended to test the claims against Snap and the other companies and potentially influence how similar cases are resolved. The next bellwether trials are scheduled to begin in March, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers. A Snap spokesperson said in a statement that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts, and remains committed to “continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." Plaintiffs S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll.  The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves.  Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts brought by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide.  In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million in damages. The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies. The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies. In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over claims its platforms harmed teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. The deal conditioned $5 billion of the payout on the states reaching similar settlements with Snap, TikTok and YouTube.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 : A group representing nearly all major automakers on Monday urged US lawmakers to pass a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles when they return next week for a quick session after the midterm congressional elections. In September, the Senate sponsors of the bipartisan effort to ban Chinese vehicles agreed to delay an effort to fast-track the measure until November. "We need to protect the U.S. market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in American communities," said John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major automakers.

Nov 2 : Russian owners of non-state data centres will be required to reserve 10 per cent of their capacity to help keep Russia's IT infrastructure running, according to a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on Monday. This mechanism would allow Russian authorities to quickly access available data centre capacity if needed. Russian data centres have become targets of Ukrainian drone attacks in recent weeks, with facilities operated by technology companies Yandex and Sberbank struck in October. Putin instructed the Digital Development Ministry to conduct an inventory of available capacity and floor space at privately owned data centres across Russia.

LONDON, Nov 2 : Google parent Alphabet is selling €6 billion ($6.7 billion) of bonds on Monday, according to a memo from one of the deal's managers, testing investor appetite after doubts about the AI trade triggered a recent selloff in tech stocks and debt. Alphabet is offering the new bonds in seven tranches, with total demand just over €17 billion, the memo from one of the banks arranging the sale seen by Reuters showed.  The bonds, expected to be priced later on Monday, have maturities ranging from 2 to 19 years. They include one floating-rate tranche and six fixed-rate tranches, according to an SEC filing. The offer marks Alphabet's second euro-denominated sale this year. In May, it sold €9 billion of bonds across six tranches, following a rare 100-year sterling bond sale in February.

Concerns about the financing required to support heavy spending on artificial intelligence, and the returns needed to justify that investment, have weighed on technology stocks and bonds in recent weeks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5 per cent in October. The latest bout of volatility has been fuelled by disappointing quarterly results from Alphabet and Amazon, two of the biggest spenders on data centres. Alphabet said it intended to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include repaying outstanding debt. Barclays, BNP Paribas and Deutsche Bank are the joint book-running managers for the offering, according to the SEC filing. Alphabet's shares fell more than 12 per cent last Thursday, their worst day ever, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market value after its quarterly results showed slower-than-expected growth in Google Search and cash burn that rattled investors. For the whole year, the company expects capital spending of as much as $205 billion. As of September 30, Alphabet had also signed leases, mainly for data centres, that have not yet commenced, with future payments of $130.5 billion that are not yet recorded on its balance sheet, the SEC filing showed. Microsoft, by contrast, was the only Big Tech company generating cash in the quarter. Still, analysts expect major tech companies to step up bond sales in Europe to fund infrastructure investment, tapping the region's deep and liquid debt markets. Alphabet shares were up about 1 per cent in premarket trading. The company's US-listed shares fell nearly 19 per cent in October, their worst monthly performance on record. Its dollar-denominated 4.1 per cent bond due in 2031 was little changed on Monday at about 95.43 cents on the dollar. ($1 = 0.8948 euros)

Source: Reuters

Nov 2 : Oracle plans to raise $20 billion through bond and share sales, regulatory filings showed on Monday, as the software giant taps investors to fund its costly AI and cloud infrastructure build-out. Shares of the company fell nearly 6 per cent, extending a roughly 33 per cent decline this year through Friday. Oracle said it would use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including capital spending, debt repayment, acquisitions, dividends and share buybacks. The fundraising underscores the scale of Oracle's AI investment as it seeks to more than triple revenue by fiscal 2030. The company said last week that capital spending would peak this fiscal year and the next, while pledging to raise no more than $20 billion in additional financing for AI through fiscal 2030.

Oracle had $125.34 billion in notes payable and other borrowings as of August 31, compared with fiscal 2026 revenue of $67.36 billion. It expects revenue to exceed $225 billion and adjusted earnings to top $21 per share in fiscal 2030.  Wall Street expects the company's adjusted profit per share for fiscal 2027 to be $8.14, according to data compiled by LSEG. The bond offering comprises six tranches maturing between 2029 and 2046, including one floating-rate tranche and five fixed-rate tranches. Interest rates, prices and the number of shares have not been set. Oracle’s existing 6.85 per cent bonds due in 2066 fell more than 1.2 cents on the dollar, according to Tradeweb data.  Investors have focused on Oracle's AI spending because it lacks the revenue scale of cloud rivals Microsoft and Amazon and has significant exposure to OpenAI, the loss-making developer of ChatGPT.

NEW YORK, Nov 2 : The dollar eased on Monday as oil prices plunged and Treasury yields retreated ahead of a week full of catalysts, including the US midterm elections, a host of data on the US labor market and multiple central bank rate decisions. Crude prices tumbled about 7 per cent as continuing talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on ending the US-Israeli war with Iran lifted hopes for reduced disruptions to supply from the Middle East. The easing of oil prices initially helped buoy US equities, although technology stocks were weaker again as iPhone maker Apple dipped about 2 per cent ahead of its quarterly earnings and Oracle slumped more than 8 per cent on plans to raise $20 billion through bond and share sales. Growing concerns about massive spending by companies on the emerging AI technology have weighed on stocks in recent weeks, helping to support the dollar as a safe-haven play.

Oil prices, the December WTI tested 105 on Friday, and we're below 100 now," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets in New York. "When we went into the weekend, everything looked bad. Stocks had sold off, oil was at new contract highs in the December WTI. And we come back from the weekend, and this is a collective sigh of relief." The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.22 per cent to 101.76after declining to 101.42, its lowest since September 30. The euro was up 0.3 per cent at $1.1192, even after late Friday's revision by Fitch of France's outlook to "negative" from "stable" on worsening debt dynamics. MANUFACTURING INDEX RISES IN OCTOBER On the data front, the Institute for Supply Management said its manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) increased to 55.5 last month from 54.5 in September, while input prices remained elevated. Markets will also deal with a flurry of data on the labor market this week, culminating on Friday with the government's key October payrolls report. The S&P Global Eurozone Manufacturing PMI showed manufacturing activity growth in the region held up well in October, albeit easing as new order growth slowed and rising costs from energy and supply-chain disruptions squeezed margins. Multiple central banks are scheduled to issue policy statements this week, including those in Britain, Australia, Norway and Sweden. CRYPTO MARKETS STEADY AFTER BINANCE HACK In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 1.5 per cent to $76,645.42 and ether declined 1.14 per cent to $2,236.50, steadying slightly but remaining near lows hit last week following the record $6.3 billion heist at Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange. Binance's customers have withdrawn almost $5 billion from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened after the hack, the company said. Americans head to the polls on Tuesday to determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from US President Donald Trump's Republican Party, with the economy and high prices key issues among voters. Democrats are widely predicted to win the House of Representatives, but wresting control of the Senate may prove more difficult. Sterling strengthened 0.1 per cent to $1.3406. PMI data showed British manufacturers started the final quarter of 2026 with the strongest output growth in more than two years, although fast-rising costs may worry the Bank of England, which looks set to raise interest rates this week. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar strengthened 0.23 per cent to 157.89. Japan's real interest rates have risen recently, especially in the long- and super-long zones, the central bank said in a full version of its quarterly outlook report.

Nov 2 : SpaceX is in talks to buy EchoStar's wireless service Boost Mobile or gain access to its network, which it leases from AT&T and T-mobile, the Washington Post reported on Monday. SpaceX has held talks with telecom firm EchoStar in recent months about launching its own signature wireless service through a deal with the company, the report said, citing people familiar with the negotiations. The move would support the Elon Musk-led company's plans to build a hybrid satellite-terrestrial mobile network through Starlink Mobile, combining its satellite constellation with ground-based infrastructure to challenge US wireless giants AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. Telecom stocks came under pressure following SpaceX's $8 billion spectrum deal, as investors assessed the threat posed by a new satellite-powered wireless competitor.

Acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network could give SpaceX a ready-made subscriber base and distribution platform to accelerate its plans. EchoStar had 7.38 million wireless subscribers at the end of the second quarter, primarily consisting of Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile customers. Musk has discussed the deal personally, meeting with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month, the Washington Post's report said. The proposed service may need consent from AT&T and T-Mobile, as Boost Mobile's existing network-leasing agreements may not be transferable to a new owner without the carriers' approval, the report said. SpaceX and EchoStar did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. EchoStar shares rose about 3.4 per cent in premarket trading, while T-Mobile slipped 2 per cent. AT&T and Verizon also edged lower. Analysts and industry experts have pointed to the challenges SpaceX might face in building a network that could become the fourth-largest wireless carrier in the US. The rocket and satellite company will likely need to invest heavily in ground infrastructure, customer service, handset subsidies and promotions — costly areas of the wireless business where the Big Three already have extensive operations.

Source: Reuters
